title: About
text:
Presenting the GLEAM dashboard at FAO's World Food Forum, Rome, 2023
I’m a humanitarian researcher and GIS and data specialist. Over seven years with IMPACT Initiatives (REACH), ICRC and FAO, I’ve worked on needs assessments, displacement and market monitoring, climate and remote sensing, and emissions modelling, across sectors from food security and water and sanitation to protection and education.
I started with IMPACT Initiatives (REACH) in Ukraine and then South Sudan, where over three years I went from Junior GIS Officer to GIS Specialist. There I managed a team of six, ran a satellite-based climate monitoring system, and worked with South Sudan’s National Bureau of Statistics on the national FSNMS household survey. At FAO in Rome I analysed livestock emissions with GLEAM and designed a geospatial data warehouse on Google Cloud. At ICRC in Ukraine I was the delegation’s GIS and data focal point, using remote sensing in ArcGIS Pro and Google Earth Engine to monitor floods, crops and critical sites near the frontline, and managed a team of three. I’m now a Senior Research Officer with IMPACT Initiatives (REACH), leading the 2026 needs assessment for northern Nigeria from Dakar.

title: Flood and drought monitoring from satellite data
text:
The challenge
South Sudan had successive years of severe flooding from 2019 to 2021, with drought in other parts of the country. Much of the affected area was hard to reach on the ground, and partners needed regular, consistent information on where flooding and drought were happening and where they were likely to strike again.

title: Flood and drought monitoring from satellite data
text:
What I did

Built the monitoring: a system in Google Earth Engine, written in Python, combining CHIRPS rainfall, NDVI vegetation data and satellite flood extent mapped by image classification.
Ran it every month for more than two years, across South Sudan and several East African countries.
Turned it into products: monthly data, quarterly factsheets, a dashboard, and static and story maps.
Checked it on the ground: led three field assessments after extreme floods, verifying the flood mapping and documenting impacts on livelihoods.

title: Flood and drought monitoring from satellite data
text:
Outcome

Used by OCHA, the clusters and partners, and fed the mission’s wider shocks monitoring.
Early-warning reports on long-term flood trends identified areas likely to flood again.




Rainfall, vegetation and flood extent were processed each month in Google Earth Engine and turned into data, factsheets, a dashboard and maps.

title: A 32,000-household needs assessment under access constraints
text:
The challenge
A Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA) is a large household survey whose findings help decide where humanitarian aid goes. In 2026 the northern Nigeria MSNA had to reach displaced people, refugees and host communities across 11 states, where insecurity put large areas out of reach, with more than 20 partners collecting up to 1,000 interviews a day.

title: A 32,000-household needs assessment under access constraints
text:
What I did

Sampling: designed a two-stage cluster sample that kept coverage despite insecurity, and a resampling process that replaced unreachable clusters during fieldwork without breaking the design.
Monitoring and cleaning: built an automated R and Python system that checked up to 1,000 submissions a day, with cleaning logs, a follow-up list for each partner and a live progress dashboard.
Coordination: coordinated data collection with more than 20 partners and worked with Nigeria’s National Bureau of Statistics.
The full cycle: took the assessment from secondary data review and methodology to analysis and reporting.

title: A 32,000-household needs assessment under access constraints
text:
Outcome

Findings presented to Nigeria’s Cadre Harmonisé food security analysis, and being presented to partners, donors, clusters and agency heads.
Each stage rebuilt as a public, runnable repository on synthetic data, so the methods can be seen without exposing survey data.




The monitoring dashboard’s progress page, as used on the real survey, running on synthetic data.






The sample after two rounds of resampling: sampled, replacement and inaccessible clusters. Synthetic data, not real findings.
